title: Building Reusable Evaluation Frameworks for Agentic AI Products
gist: Elastic's principal data scientist describes consolidating siloed agent evaluations into a shared framework built on tracing, LLM-as-judge plus deterministic evaluators, and TypeScript/Playwright. Domain-expert datasets and evaluator calibration remained team-owned and could not be abstracted.

insights.claim: Evaluating only an agent's end result hides mid-run failures such as querying the wrong database, so granular tracing of tool calls and retrievals is a prerequisite for actionable evals.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Observability/tracing vendors become the data layer for agent quality; tracing is a buy-or-build wedge.

insights.claim: Elastic trialed several tracing tools (LangSmith, Phoenix, its own Elastic Observability) because the market moved fast and early LLM-specific tracing was immature, so data ended up stored in different places.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: LLM-tracing tooling is fragmented and unsettled; incumbents' observability lacked LLM-specific features out of the box.

insights.claim: User feedback such as a thumbs-down can be added to a test dataset so future agent iterations are regression-tested on past failures; LangSmith's Add to Dataset feature supports this loop.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Production feedback to eval-set flywheel is a product feature that drives tool stickiness.

insights.claim: Where full telemetry cannot be captured (restricted industries, enterprise customers sharing redacted data), teams must rely on proxy signals and explicit or implicit feedback, as in recommender systems.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Enterprise data-sharing limits cap vendor visibility into agent quality; feedback UX becomes strategic.

insights.claim: Tool choice for agent tracing depends on what storage a company already has (e.g. teams with MLflow use it for agents), not necessarily on tool maturity.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Incumbent MLOps and observability stacks have a distribution advantage in agent tracing.

insights.claim: Elastic teams building security agents and enterprise chatbots each created their own datasets, evaluators, trace stores and eval locations, creating duplicated effort that later required consolidation.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Siloed agent evals are the default failure mode in large orgs; shared tooling is a cost saver.
insights.locator: AI Agents We Are Running in Production

insights.claim: A shared framework with dataset import, a standardized schema, trace-based evaluators (token usage, latency, tool calls), shared RAG evaluators and custom evaluators let a new agent (AI rules generation) get evals spun up quickly.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Reusable eval building blocks lower marginal cost of shipping each new agent.

insights.claim: An eval run flows dataset input/output into a task (agent run), then code-based, LLM-as-judge and trace-based evaluators, with results stored back into Elastic or other tools.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Defines the standard agent eval pipeline that vendors compete to host.

insights.claim: Common metrics consolidated across teams were precision/recall, semantic similarity and factuality, e.g. checking for hallucinated product IDs or nonexistent MITRE attack tactics.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Hallucination of domain identifiers is the concrete risk evals target in enterprise agents.

insights.claim: Elastic built shared tooling by starting ad hoc and consolidating later, arguing that two months of upfront planning would have meant shipping far less.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Speed-first then consolidate is the practical path in fast markets; premature abstraction costs shipping velocity.

insights.claim: Evals were run on a customized Playwright runner called Scout in TypeScript to match the TypeScript production codebase, and can run locally with scores printed in the terminal.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Evals are migrating into the software engineering test stack rather than staying in data-science notebooks.

insights.claim: Data scientists ported Python eval tooling to TypeScript using Claude and Cursor with review by experienced TypeScript engineers, which let the data science team contribute directly to shared frameworks.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: AI coding tools erode language barriers between data science and product engineering teams.

insights.claim: Chang is only half-convinced she would skip the Python framework if starting over, but would not have started with TypeScript and judges the later move a good long-run decision.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Matching production stack matters, but starting in a familiar language speeds early learning.

insights.claim: LLM-as-judge works well for ambiguous and open-ended tasks such as brand tone, coherence and style, and can explain its grading via chain-of-thought, provided it is paired with hybrid evaluations.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Hybrid judge-plus-rules grading is the emerging production standard.

insights.claim: LLM-as-judge is weak on granularity, structured outputs such as JSON, YAML or query languages, internal facts like product IDs, and shows run-to-run variance even with the same model.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Judge-only eval stacks are unreliable for structured enterprise outputs.

insights.claim: Rules-based or programmatic evals are unambiguous, cheap and fast and need no LLM call, but are hard to scale to natural language or open-ended answers.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Deterministic checks cut eval cost; judge calls are reserved for text that needs them.

insights.claim: Using the same model family to judge itself biases results: Meta and CrowdStrike found Llama judging Llama rated Llama models higher.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Self-preference bias means cross-vendor judges are needed for credible model comparisons.

insights.claim: Elastic reports its internal LLM-as-judge findings after a year or two were validated by an Anthropic blog released in January that covered similar points on model-based graders.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Practitioner knowledge on agent evals is converging across labs and vendors.

insights.claim: Elastic must make sure its AI agents generate correct ES|QL syntax, and builds tool calls into agents to format or check queries, comparing outputs against known-good answers in test datasets.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Vendors owning a query language must evaluate agent code generation for their own DSL.
insights.locator: AI Agents We Are Running in Production

themes.theme: What cannot be abstracted: domain expertise and calibration

insights.claim: Bespoke dataset creation cannot be automated into a shared framework; security analysts and researchers, not engineers or data scientists, must define what a working security agent looks like.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Domain-expert labelling is the durable bottleneck and moat in vertical agents.

insights.claim: A security agent update caused it to flag attacks even on entirely benign data, and the eval set was then fixed to catch the over-aggressive regression.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Agent regressions can be false-positive inflation, not just quality loss; evals need benign scenarios.

insights.claim: Evaluator calibration, meaning consistent scores across repeat runs and agreement with human evaluators, cannot be provided by a shared framework; poorly calibrated evaluators produce junk.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Eval trustworthiness depends on per-team human alignment work, limiting turnkey eval products.

insights.claim: LLMs were used to scale up test datasets but anchored to real domain expertise and user needs, such as analysts spinning up VMs and Okta test environments.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Synthetic data scales evals only when seeded from real expert scenarios.

insights.claim: Regression is agent-specific and what counts as positive or negative behavior is discovered iteratively, so it is hard to predict upfront in ambiguous workflows.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Eval suites are living assets that need ongoing investment.

themes.theme: Practical adoption guidance and release gating

insights.claim: For first agents, a test dataset of just 20 to 50 records is enough to start, and ad hoc evals are fine, because evaluation evidence justifies further investment in agents.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Low barrier to first evals means adoption is not gated by dataset cost.

insights.claim: Leadership will start asking how agents are performing and users will hit production problems, so at least one eval or tracing setup should exist even with few agents.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Eval and observability spend follows production agent deployments.

insights.claim: Elastic gates releases with a weighted composite score over granular metrics (precision, recall, factuality) against a threshold, followed by manual smoke testing, which she calls rigorous but also not really.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Even a leading vendor's agent release gate is a simple weighted score plus manual check, so agent QA is immature.

insights.claim: Elastic customers reportedly ingest petabytes of data for cybersecurity use, with one huge banking customer cited, making log-reading agents a natural application layer on top of existing data stores.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Agents layered on incumbent data stores in security and observability extend vendor TAM.
insights.locator: AI Agents We Are Running in Production

insights.claim: Elastic is also consolidating its separate security agents into one workflow that identifies which agent is being addressed, rather than a dropdown, paralleling the consolidation of evals.
insights.speaker: Susan Chang
insights.so_what: Agent sprawl within a product pushes vendors toward unified agent experiences.
